title: Massive Star-Forming Region in 30 Doradus (Hubble)
caption: Star cluster R136 in the 30 Doradus nebula, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: 30 Doradus, 30 Dor, Tarantula Nebula · constellation Dorado · about 170,000 light-years away (source figure)
credit: Image: NASA, ESA, Elena Sabbi (ESA, STScI); Acknowledgment: SOC-WFC3, Robert O'Connell (UVA)

recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: A dense cluster of bright blue-white stars sits among fluffy orange and brown clouds. The cluster is R136, a massive young stellar grouping inside the 30 Doradus nebula, also called the Tarantula Nebula. It lies about 170,000 light-years away in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way, in the constellation Dorado.

30 Doradus is a turbulent region where stars are being born. Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 recorded it through several filters, and the colours carry meaning. Blue comes from the hottest, most massive stars, green from glowing oxygen, and red from fluorescing hydrogen.

Because it is close by, this stellar nursery gives astronomers insight into the life cycle of stars, and it hints at how star clusters may have come together in the early universe. A nebula like this is a cloud of gas and dust where new stars form, and the young stars in turn light up the gas around them.

understand.summary: Hubble's WFC3 took this image. NASA shows F336W and F438W in blue, F555W in green, F814W in red, and the hydrogen-alpha filter F656N in orange-red.
understand.eye: Exposures adding up to many hours gather far more light than the eye can, and some of the data comes from ultraviolet light, which the eye cannot see.

explore: Hubble collected the data between 20 and 27 October 2009, with exposure times of 11.7 hours for the ultraviolet-visible channel and 2.6 hours for the infrared channel of Wide Field Camera 3.
